Quick validation and a few operational notes for Jeanne (pasting below so we have a single thread reply). Numbers in the CSV are summarized; below are the testing assumptions and failure modes we saw during synthetic capacity sweeps: 

- Node configs: A100-40GB per node; model quantization profiles were executed via our runtime path that uses int8 matmul kernels where applicable.
- Throughput/concurrency: for Redwood-7B-quant a single node sustained ~2200 input tokens/s at 512-out with 4 concurrent streams (p50 ~12ms/token). At 8 nodes we saw near-linear scaling for steady-state throughput; tail-latency p99 improvement is sub-linear due to burst amplification in scheduler queue depth.
- Burst scenarios: We ran 30s bursts at 10x baseline QPS. Short bursts primarily cause scheduler queue depth to spike. We observed three degradation paths: (1) graceful queueing with increased latency; (2) backpressure where client receives 429s if request queue is full (configurable); (3) transient OOMs only when active batch sizes spike on fp16 and memory headroom is <10%. Our recommended mitigation: enable request rejection at the 95th percentile of queue depth + autoscale cooldown of 45s.
- Warmup/KV-caching: priming reduces p99 by ~25% for chat-style workloads; for pure stateless text-gen savings are smaller (~8%).
- Measurement windows: reported p99/p95 taken over 5–10 minute steady windows (not the burst window). Burst metrics reported separately to avoid masking tail effects.

Operational caveat for Atlas: if you plan long tail distributions with >20% requests >1024 tokens, consider using 13B quant variant on 4+ nodes to avoid throttling during bursts.

I also attached a short PDF that graphs capacity-sweep curves and shows our recommended SLO guardrails.
